chapterNote: Chapter 25 opens the second great Solomonic collection — proverbs copied out two centuries later by the scholars of King Hezekiah (v.1). It begins where the book began, with kings: the searching glory of the throne (vv.2-3), the refining-out of the wicked that establishes it (vv.4-5), and the courtier's wisdom of humility before it (vv.6-7). From the king's court the proverbs widen into the everyday court of common life — the lawsuit you should not rush (vv.8-10), the well-timed word that gleams like gold (vv.11-15), and a string of vivid comparisons on restraint, neighborliness, and self-control. The chapter closes where Solomon's wisdom always lands: the man who cannot rule his own spirit is a city with its walls breached (v.28).

1.text: Here are more of Solomon's proverbs — the ones that the scholars serving Hezekiah, king of Judah, gathered and set down.
1.amp: These also are proverbs [mashal — pithy comparisons that set one thing beside another to teach] of Solomon, which the men [enosh — the men, here the scholars] of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out [ataq — moved over, transcribed from an older source].
1.notes: mashal (H4912) is the book's signature genre, the comparison-saying. This editorial note marks the start of the second Solomonic collection (chs. 25-29): some two hundred years after Solomon, Hezekiah's men (cf. 2 Kgs 18) gathered and transcribed (ataq, H6275) sayings that had survived from his vast output (1 Kgs 4:32).

2.text: It is the glory of God to conceal a matter, but the glory of kings is to search a matter out.
2.amp: It is the glory [kavod — weight, honor, splendor] of God [Elohim] to conceal [satar — hide away, keep secret] a thing [dabar — word, matter], but the glory of kings is to search out [chaqar — explore, probe to the bottom] a matter.
2.notes: kavod (H3519) is honor that has 'weight'; the same word frames both halves, but the glories differ. God's majesty is shown by what He hides (satar, H5641; cf. Deut 29:29); a king's by his diligence to investigate (chaqar, H2713). The verse is no contradiction but a division of labor between heaven's hiddenness and the throne's responsibility to discern.

3.text: The heavens for height, and the earth for depth — so the heart of kings is past searching out.
3.amp: The heavens [shamayim] for height, and the earth [eretz] for depth [omeq — deepness, the unplumbed], so the heart [leb] of kings is unsearchable [literally 'there is no searching it out'].
3.notes: a three-fold comparison: as no man measures the height of the sky or the depth of the ground, so the inner counsel of a king (leb, H3820) lies beyond reach. omeq (H6011) is depth, the unfathomable. The verse both praises the king's discretion and, paired with v.2, warns the subject not to presume he has read the throne's mind.

4.text: Take away the dross from the silver, and a vessel comes forth for the refiner;
4.amp: Take away [hagah — remove, purge out] the dross [sig — the scum and impurity] from the silver [keseph], and a vessel [keli — an article, instrument] comes forth for the refiner [tsaraph — the smelter who refines and tests by fire].
4.notes: sig (H5509) is the worthless slag that fire drives off; keseph (H3701) is silver, prized only once purged. This is the first half of a paired proverb (with v.5): the metallurgist's craft becomes a parable of the throne — skim off the dross and the metal is fit for the master's use; tsaraph (H6884) is to refine and to test.

5.text: Clear the wicked out of the king's presence, and on righteousness his throne will stand firm.
5.amp: Take away [hagah — the same purging verb as v.4] the wicked [rasha — the guilty, the lawless] from before [panim — the face, presence] the king, and his throne [kisse] will be established [kun — set firm, made secure] in righteousness [tsedek].
5.notes: the proverb completes v.4: the rasha (H7563) is the dross of the realm, and purging him from the king's presence (panim, H6440) is the assaying that leaves a throne fit for use. kun (H3559), to make firm, and tsedek (H6664), righteousness, name the only foundation that holds a kingdom (cf. 16:12; 29:14): not raw power but justice.

6.text: Do not parade yourself in the presence of the king, nor take your stand in the place of the great;
6.amp: Do not glorify yourself [hadar — honor, exalt, make yourself grand] in the presence [panim] of the king, and do not stand [amad — take up a position, plant yourself] in the place [maqom] of the great [gadol — the mighty, the eminent];
6.notes: hadar (H1921) is to honor or adorn — here, reflexively, to put oneself forward as impressive. The court is a place of rank, and amad (H5975), to take one's stand, in the maqom (H4725) reserved for the gadol (H1419) is to seize an honor not granted. The verse begins the famous lesson on humility that Jesus draws on directly in Luke 14:8-11.

7.text: for it is better that he say to you, "Come up here," than that you be put lower before a noble whom your own eyes have seen.
7.amp: for it is better [tov] that it be said to you, "Come up [alah — ascend, come higher] here," than that you be brought low [shaphel — humbled, set down] in the presence [panim] of the prince [nadiv — the noble, the generous-hearted] whom your eyes [ayin] have seen.
7.notes: the wisdom of self-lowering: better to be called up (alah, H5927) than to be set down (shaphel, H8213) in public shame. nadiv (H5081) is a noble, one whose rank is unquestioned. To take the high seat and be demoted before a man you can plainly see is the very reversal Jesus warns against — 'whoever exalts himself will be humbled' (Luke 14:11).

8.text: Do not rush out to go to court, or what will you do in the end, when your neighbor has put you to shame?
8.amp: Do not go out [yatsa] hastily [mahar — in a rush, without weighing it] to contend [rib — bring suit, take to law], lest you not know what to do [asah] in the end [acharit — the latter outcome, how it finishes], when your neighbor [rea] has put you to shame [kalam — humiliated, disgraced you].
8.notes: rib (H7378) is to press a legal dispute; mahar (H4118) is the haste that skips the cost-counting. The wisdom looks to the acharit (H319), the end of the matter: a quarrel rushed to court can boomerang in public disgrace (kalam, H3637) when your rea (H7453) exposes your case. Count the finish before you file.

9.text: Argue your case with your neighbor himself, but do not betray another's confidence,
9.amp: Debate [rib — press, plead] your cause [riv — your dispute, controversy] with your neighbor [rea] himself, and do not uncover [galah — reveal, lay bare] the secret [sod — the confidence, the private counsel] of another;
9.notes: the remedy to the rash lawsuit of v.8: settle it privately, face to face. rib (H7378) returns, but now contained between the two parties. galah (H1540) is to uncover; sod (H5475) is intimate, confidential counsel. To win an argument by spilling a third party's secret is to trade one wrong for another — and v.10 names the cost.

10.text: lest the one who hears it bring shame upon you, and your ill repute never depart.
10.amp: lest the one who hears [shama] it shame [chasad — here in its rarer sense, reproach, put to shame] you, and your evil report [dibbah — bad name, slander against you] never turn away [shub — return, depart].
10.notes: the betrayer of confidence (v.9) is overheard, and the disgrace sticks. dibbah (H1681) is an evil report or bad reputation; once it attaches it does not 'turn back' (shub, H7725), the very verb usually meaning repent or return. A loose tongue in a quarrel can brand a man for life.

11.text: Speak the right word at just the right moment, and it gleams like golden apples set within frames of silver filigree.
11.amp: A word [dabar] fitly spoken [ophen — 'upon its wheels,' at just the right turn and timing] is like apples [tappuach] of gold [zahab] in carved settings [maskith — ornamental filigree, a worked silver frame] of silver [keseph].
11.notes: the Hebrew literally reads 'a word spoken upon its wheels' (ophen, H655) — a word that turns smoothly into place at the right moment. dabar (H1697), the right word at the right time, is a jewel: golden fruit framed in silver filigree (maskith, H4906). It is not only what is said but the timing that makes it precious (cf. 15:23).

12.text: Like a ring of gold and an ornament of fine gold is a wise reprover to a listening ear.
12.amp: Like an earring [nezem] of gold [zahab] and an ornament [chali — a jewel, fine adornment] of fine gold [kethem — the purest, most prized gold], so is a wise [chakam] reprover [yakach — one who corrects and rebukes] to a hearing [shama — attentive, obedient] ear [ozen].
12.notes: kethem (H3800) is the costliest grade of gold. A wise rebuke (yakach, H3198) lands on a teachable ear (ozen that does shama, H8085) not as an insult but as fine jewelry — something that adorns the one who receives it. Both halves of the gift must meet: a wise corrector and a willing hearer.

13.text: A trustworthy messenger is, to the ones who sent him, like snow's coolness amid the heat of harvest — he brings their very souls back to life.
13.amp: Like the cold [tsinnah] of snow [sheleg] in the time [yom] of harvest [qatsir], so is a faithful [aman — trustworthy, firm, reliable] messenger [tsir] to those who send [shalach] him, for he refreshes [shub — restores, brings back] the soul [nephesh] of his masters [adon].
13.notes: not snow falling in harvest (which would ruin the crop), but the cooling of snow brought down from the heights to refresh laborers in the scorching heat. aman (H539) is the root of faithfulness and trust. A reliable messenger (tsir) restores (shub, H7725) the very life (nephesh, H5315) of the one who sent him — a rare and reviving thing.

14.text: Like clouds and wind without rain is one who boasts of gifts he never gives.
14.amp: Like clouds and wind [ruach — wind, breath] without rain [geshem], so is a man [ish] who boasts [halal — praises himself, brags] of a false [sheqer — a lying, deceptive] gift [mattath — a present, a thing supposedly given].
14.notes: in a parched land, gathering clouds and a freshening wind promise rain — and the disappointment when none falls is bitter. So the man who boasts (halal, H1984) of a gift (mattath, H4991) that is sheqer (H8267), false, raises hope and then withholds. His generosity is all show, all wind.

15.text: By patience a ruler is won over, and a gentle tongue can break a bone.
15.amp: By long [orek — length, slowness] of forbearance [aph — literally the nose, the seat of anger; slowness to anger] a ruler [qatsin — a commander, chief] is persuaded [pathah — won over, opened up], and a soft [rak — gentle, tender] tongue [lashon] breaks [shabar — shatters] the bone [gerem].
15.notes: 'long of nose' (erek aph, H753 + H639) is the Hebrew idiom for patience — the opposite of the short-tempered 'hot nose.' Patient persuasion (pathah, H6601) bends even a hardened ruler (qatsin, H7101), and a gentle (rak, H7390) tongue can break (shabar, H7665) bone — the paradox that the softest speech carries the hardest force (cf. 15:1).

16.text: Have you found honey? Eat only what is enough for you, lest you be glutted with it and vomit it up.
16.amp: Have you found [matsa] honey [devash]? Eat [akal] only what is sufficient [day — enough, your measure] for you, lest you be sated [saba — filled to the full] with it and vomit [qa] it up.
16.notes: devash (H1706), honey, is good — but the good thing taken past its measure (day, H1767) turns to sickness. saba (H7646) is to be over-full. This proverb on moderation is paired with v.27 (too much honey, too much self-glory); even legitimate sweetness must know its limit.

17.text: Let your foot be rarely in your neighbor's house, lest he grow weary of you and hate you.
17.amp: Make precious [yaqar — make rare, withhold and prize] your foot [regel] from your neighbor's [rea] house [bayit], lest he be sated [saba — full to weariness] with you, and hate [sane] you.
17.notes: yaqar (H3365) means to be precious or rare; the counsel is to make your visits scarce so they stay valued. The same 'fullness' verb as v.16, saba (H7646), reappears — a neighbor overfed with your company grows sick of you and turns to hatred (sane, H8130). Even good fellowship spoils when it overstays.

18.text: Like a war-club, a sword, and a sharp arrow is a man who bears false witness against his neighbor.
18.amp: A man [ish] who answers [anah — testifies, gives evidence] as a false [sheqer] witness [ed] against his neighbor [rea] is a war-club [mephits — a heavy maul], and a sword [chereb], and a sharpened [shanan — honed to a point] arrow [chets].
18.notes: the false witness (ed sheqer, H5707 + H8267) is named as three weapons at once — a crushing club, a slashing sword, a piercing arrow, ranged from close to far. anah (H6030) is the courtroom verb 'to testify.' Perjury is no mere word-crime; it is assault, breaking the ninth commandment as violence against a neighbor's life and name.

19.text: Like a broken tooth or a foot out of joint is confidence in a faithless man in the day of trouble.
19.amp: Confidence [mivtach — trust, reliance, security] in a treacherous man [bagad — one who deals faithlessly, a betrayer] in the day [yom] of trouble [tsarah — distress, the pinch of crisis] is like a broken [raah — bad, decayed] tooth [shen], and a foot [regel] out of joint [maad — slipping, that gives way].
19.notes: mivtach (H4009) is the trust one leans on — and to lean it on a bagad (H898), a betrayer, precisely when tsarah (H6869) strikes, is to bite down on a rotten tooth or step on a foot that slips. The very member meant to bear weight fails at the moment of need. Crisis is when false friendship is exposed.

20.text: Like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, like vinegar poured on soda, is the one who sings songs to a heavy heart.
20.amp: Like one who takes away [adah — removes, strips off] a garment [beged] on a cold day [yom], and like vinegar [chomets] upon soda [nether — natron, lye], so is one who sings [shir] songs [shir] to a heavy [ra — bad, grieving, sour] heart [leb].
20.notes: two pictures of unwelcome mismatch: stripping a coat in the cold leaves a man exposed, and vinegar on natron (nether, H5427) hisses and ruins the alkali. So cheerful songs (shir, H7892) flung at a grieving heart (leb that is ra, H7451) only sharpen the pain. Wisdom reads the moment; misjudged gladness wounds (cf. Rom 12:15).

21.text: Should the one who hates you go hungry, set bread before him to eat; should he be parched, hand him water to drink.
21.amp: If the one who hates [sane — your enemy, the one hostile to you] you is hungry [raeb], give him bread [lechem — food, grain] to eat [akal]; and if he is thirsty [tsame], give him water [mayim] to drink [shaqah].
21.notes: sane (H8130), to hate, names the enemy — yet the command is to feed and water him. lechem (H3899) is bread, the basic gift of life. This radical mercy, paired with v.22, is quoted by Paul as the Christian's response to evil: not retaliation but active good toward the one who wrongs you (Rom 12:20).

22.text: For by doing so you rake burning coals together upon his head, and the LORD Himself will repay you.
22.amp: For you will heap [chatah — gather and rake up] coals of fire [gechalim] upon his head [rosh], and the LORD [YHWH] will reward [shalam — repay, make complete] you.
22.notes: the 'coals of fire' (gechalim, H1513) are best read not as vengeance but as the burning shame of conscience that kindness lights in an enemy — or perhaps a borrowed image of contrition, coals carried on the head. chatah (H2846) is to rake up. The promise is that YHWH (H3068) Himself shall repay (shalam, H7999) the one who overcomes evil with good (cf. Rom 12:20-21).

23.text: The north wind brings forth rain, and a secretive tongue, angry faces.
23.amp: The north [tsaphon] wind [ruach] drives forth [chul — whirls out, brings to birth] rain [geshem], so a backbiting [sether — 'of the hidden,' the secret slanderer] tongue [lashon] brings an indignant [zaam — enraged, denouncing] face [panim].
23.notes: as surely as a certain wind produces a certain weather, a tongue working in secret (sether, H5643, 'hiddenness') produces a storm of indignant faces (panim that zaam, H2194). chul (H2342) is to whirl forth, even to give birth. The slanderer thinks his words vanish unseen; in fact they reliably brew open anger.

24.text: It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a shared house with a quarrelsome wife.
24.amp: It is better [tov] to dwell [yashab — sit, remain, settle] in the corner [pinnah] of the housetop [gag], than with a contentious [madon — strife-making, quarrelsome] woman [ishshah] in a house [bayit] shared.
24.notes: tov (H2896), 'better,' frames the trade-off: a cramped, exposed roof-corner is preferable to a full house ruled by strife. madon (H4066) is contention, the spirit of endless quarreling. The proverb (repeated at 21:9) is not misogyny but a vivid verdict on what makes a home — not its size but its peace; cf. 17:1, the dry morsel with quiet.

25.text: Like cold water to a thirsty soul is good news from a far country.
25.amp: Like cold [qar] water [mayim] to a weary, thirsty [ayeph — faint, parched] soul [nephesh], so is a good [tov] report [shemuah — news, tidings] from a far [merachoq] country [eretz].
25.notes: in a world without swift travel, word from a distant land (eretz, H776) came rarely and was long awaited; ayeph (H5889) is the faint thirst of the traveler. Good tidings (shemuah, H8052) to the soul that has waited for them are like cold water to the parched — reviving, life-giving. The image quietly anticipates the gospel itself as 'good news from a far country.'

26.text: Like a muddied spring or a polluted well is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked.
26.amp: Like a fouled [raphas — trampled, stirred to mud] fountain [maayan] and a ruined [shachath — corrupted, spoiled] spring [maqor], so is a righteous man [tsaddiq] who totters [mot — slips, gives way, collapses] before [panim] the wicked [rasha].
26.notes: a spring (maqor, H4726) is meant to give clean, life-sustaining water; trampled to mud (shachath, H7843) it becomes useless and harmful. So when a tsaddiq (H6662), a righteous man, caves (mot, H4131) before the rasha (H7563), the very source others depend on for refreshment is fouled. A good man's compromise poisons more than himself.

27.text: It is not good to eat too much honey; so to search out one's own glory is no glory.
27.amp: It is not good [tov] to eat [akal] much [rabah — to multiply, in excess] honey [devash]; so for men to search out [chaqar] their own glory [kavod] is not glory.
27.notes: the chapter loops back to the honey of v.16 and the searching (chaqar, H2713) of v.2 — but inverts both. Where it is a king's kavod (H3519) to search out a matter (v.2), it is no glory to search out one's own honor. Self-seeking praise, like overeaten honey (devash, H1706), sickens; glory grasped at is glory lost (cf. v.6-7; John 5:44).

28.text: Like a city broken open and left without walls is a man who has no rule over his own spirit.
28.amp: Like a city [ir] broken down [parats — breached, burst open] and without walls [chomah], so is a man [ish] who has no rule [matsar — restraint, control] over his own spirit [ruach — spirit, temper, the inner self].
28.notes: in the ancient world a city without walls (chomah, H2346) was defenseless, open to every raider. So the man who cannot rule (matsar, H4623) his own ruach (H7307) — his temper, his impulses, his inner self — is breached (parats, H6555) and exposed, plundered by every passion that comes against him. The chapter ends, as the book began, on self-governance as the heart of wisdom.
